General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW highlighted that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).
  • Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.
  • Sources indicate that by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW highlighted that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

Sources indicate that by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd.".

According to recent reports, "Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag.".

Sources indicate that marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, mentioned that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an vital factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity.".

Koehler, though, is unconvinced.

In a recent development, "You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he noted. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system.".

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

It has been revealed that the scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody.".

WADA mentioned it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation.".

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

Industry observers note that "Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place.".

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

It has been revealed that "There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been.".

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics.".

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

Mind the gap

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last few weeks, I’ve grown accustomed to waking up and experiencing low-level fear first thing in the morning.
  • Sources indicate that with any team or any squad there are players whose absence will be more keenly felt than others, but one of the things Arsenal have generally done really well in the last few years is close the gaps between ‘first choice’ and those behind them.
  • If Jurrien Timber is out, we have Ben White.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last few weeks, I’ve grown accustomed to waking up and experiencing low-level fear first thing in the morning. Today, it was a nice change not to be focused on my own health, and instead for my anxiety to centre around someone else – David Raya.

Sources indicate that with any team or any squad there are players whose absence will be more keenly felt than others, but one of the things Arsenal have generally done really well in the last few years is close the gaps between ‘first choice’ and those behind them. It doesn’t mean there isn’t still a kind of hierarchy, just that you’re better able to cope if injury or suspension hits. Mikel Arteta referencing ‘finishers’ rather than substitutes might be a psychological ploy to keep his squad happy, but it’s more easy to apply when you have the group of players he has at his disposal.

If Jurrien Timber is out, we have Ben White. If Riccardo Calafiori can’t play, Piero Hincapie can. We all worried about William Saliba needing a long lay-off after the World Cup, but the arrival of Ezri Konsa offset that in exemplary fashion. If we miss Declan Rice, we have two World Cup winners, a Brazilian international, and one of the most highly regarded young English midfielders around to fill that gap. Further forward, Noni Madueke is performing at a level that makes Bukayo Saka’s absence feel less impactful than it would have previously, and while I think forward line quality remains an concern we need to solve as urgently as January, you can flip a coin between most of our options there without feeling you’ve weakened yourself considerably.

In a recent development, unfortunately, I don’t think the same applies between the sticks. Raya has been the stand-out goalkeeper of the last few years, establishing himself as Arsenal’s number 1 after an initial settling in period. One, by the way, which I don’t think the manager handled particularly well. Typically he’s been near flawless in terms of his man-management, and while he was fundamentally right about wanting the Spaniard to come in and take the position to a new level, the way he fudged things around Aaron Ramsdale, talking about how he’d sub a goalkeeper in a game and all that nonsense really wasn’t his best moment. It left both of his keepers in a weird place for too long, until Raya’s confidence grew and his quality came to the fore.

In a recent development, since then he’s won multiple golden glove awards, his shot-stopping has been incredible at times, and although every player and every keeper will make mistakes, his have been few and far between. For me though, despite the eye-catching acrobatics – which are more easily clipped up for the social media generation – his key asset is the assurance he brings to the team. Not just when he has the ball at his feet (even if there are times I would like him to move it more quickly), but how good he is from opposition set-pieces and crosses. He comes and claims and eases pressure time and time again, and I think that’s the thing we’re going to miss most if he’s out for any significant period of time.

It has been revealed that kepa is obviously a very experienced second choice, but is second choice for a reason. Realistically though, I don’t think there’s much any club can do to have a back-up option that’s nearly as good as their number 1. If you’re being brutally honest, many clubs in the Premier League don’t have a first choice that comes anywhere close to be as good as Raya, despite their best efforts and spending millions to try and find that player. So, as anxious as I am about him being out, it is one of those things we can’t really complain about. We just have to get on with it.

Industry observers note that as I said in yesterday’s blog, we are probably going to be less secure at the back, that feels kind of inevitable, so the onus on the players further forward increases. Score more goals, turn that domination of possession and territory into more chances. If we have the ball in their half, our goalkeeper becomes something of a non-concern for as long as that’s the case. There are ways to cope, but we might need to gird our loins for some iffy moments at the back that we haven’t had to experience too often of late.

Industry observers note that as Arsenal fans though, we’ve come through worse than this with goalkeepers in the past. I don’t want to give anyone PTSD first thing on a Monday morning, but when you’ve lived what we’ve lived in seasons gone by, hopefully a little Kepa period won’t be too traumatic. And maybe, after the scan, there’ll be better news about Raya than we expect. Fingers crossed.

Industry observers note that right, I have to leave it there for this morning. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

Recent findings suggest that pod should be out around noon. Until then!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ellis Stevens | 26 Nov 2026 16:24.

Motherwell and Hibernian will come together on Saturday evening for a Scottish Premiership clash at Fir Park.

The hosts are 11th in the Scottish Premiership table with 13 points, while the visitors are ninth with 14 points.

Motherwell initially recorded a positive start to the 2026-27 Scottish Premiership season, winning two and drawing two of their first four league games under new boss Alfred Johansson.

However, the Steelmen have subsequently recorded just one win in the following 10 league fixtures, alongside two draws and seven defeats.

That run included a particularly miserable six-game losing streak from September 5 to October 25, which was eventually ended by two draws and a win at the end of October and early November.

However, another defeat last weekend, a 2-1 loss to Rangers, has culminated in Motherwell falling to 11th in the standings with just 13 points from 14 games, leaving Johansson under increasing pressure.

Motherwell's biggest problem this term has been their lack of goals, with just 16 scored in 14 league games, although they have managed to find the back of the net in each of their last four matches.

Desperate to avoid slipping further away from safety and closer to the bottom, especially with 12th-placed Kilmarnock taking on 10th-placed St Mirren, Motherwell will be eager to pick up just their fourth league win of the season on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Hibernian head into Saturday's matchday 15 encounter in resurgent form, having won three, drawn one and lost just one of their last five games across all competitions.

The first of those triumphs saw Hibernian come from behind to defeat rivals Hearts 2-1 in the Scottish League Cup semi-final, securing their place in the final and marking Marink Reedijk's first win as manager.

The subsequent two victories, 4-0 against Aberdeen and 2-1 against Dundee, have both come in the league, helping Hibernian climb out of the relegation zone and into ninth place.

Hibernian will be looking to build on that improved form with another victory on Saturday, especially as they aim to continue climbing up the table - right now trailing sixth-placed St Johnstone by just three points.

Alongside their recent run, Hibs will draw further confidence from their strength on the road this season, picking up 10 of their 14 points when playing away from home.

Hibernian are unable to call upon Felix Passlack, Kanayochukwu Megwa and Rocky Bushiri due to injury, while Nathan Lowe is a doubt.

After securing a narrow 2-1 win over Dundee last time out, Reedijk may opt to name an unchanged starting team on Saturday, including goalscorers Nicky Cadden and Martin Boyle.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugo Ekitike has been side-lined due to injury since April now.
  • The Frenchman managed to tear one the ligaments in his ankle with his return date not yet set in stone.
  • But, at the start of the season, Andoni Iraola did mention that Liverpool hope the striker is ready to feature in their final two games of the Champions League league stage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugo Ekitike has been side-lined due to injury since April now.

The Frenchman managed to tear one the ligaments in his ankle with his return date not yet set in stone.

But, at the start of the season, Andoni Iraola did mention that Liverpool hope the striker is ready to feature in their final two games of the Champions League league stage.

If he can manage to do this, the second half of the Reds' season will certainly look much more positive than the first.

However, if upon his return he isn't back to his usual self, there are some options that Liverpool can explore with a deal for a latest striker now emerging.

Gustavo Varela could become Liverpool's next Hugo Ekitike.

Last summer, a lot of people were questioning whether Liverpool had overpaid for Ekitike or not.

In the end, a deal worth around £70 million was agreed for the Frenchman with other clubs such as Newcastle United also interested in signing him.

He's performed fairly well during the 2024-25 season but, during his time with Paris Saint-Germain, things didn't really go to blueprint.

A lot of people suggested that the striker was too young and too raw for England's top flight but, fortunately, he managed to prove them all wrong.

However, Ekitike's injury set his progress back a bit with some people even suggesting that a fresh striker should be brought in to plug the gap.

Lewis Koumas eventually took up that role but, that doesn't mean that the Reds' don't have a trick or two up their sleeve, especially if this latest patch from Football Insider is to be believed.

"Liverpool will not prioritise a move to sign Monza striker Gustavo Varela in January, sources have told Football Insider," they wrote.

"The 21-year-old has emerged as a target for the Reds, having struck 11 goals from his opening 11 games in Serie A so far this term.

"The Reds are "keeping tabs" on the Portuguese youngster, with several top Italian clubs also having their "eyes fixed on him" at the moment.

"However, sources say that Varela is viewed as more of a long-term option at Anfield, and the club are not likely to make a move for him this winter.

"Monza are relaxed over their frontman's future for now, but they know that further interest from top clubs is inevitable if he continues to perform.".

Gustavo Varela could be Liverpool's next Hugo Ekitike.

Before the 2025-26 season kicked off, Gustavo Varela was a relatively unknown striker.

The 21-year-old joined Serie A outfit Monza for around €2.5 million in the summer with the deal not expected to cause that much of a stir.

However, to the surprise of many, the Portuguese attacker is currently the Serie A's top scorer.

He has 11 goals to his name and, despite all of his efforts, Monza are still sitting inside the relegation zone.

Obviously, this could just be a purple patch of form which is why the attacker is more of a long-term target rather than a short-term option.

But, if Liverpool do sign him, he could follow a similar path to Ekitike and prove the doubters wrong.

An asking price worth around €40 million has been mooted for the striker but, it's right now unclear whether the Reds would spend that much on him, even if this form does continue.

Recent findings suggest that arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, taking on Borussia Dortmund at home. It’s a game that Kepa Arrizabalaga will start in the absence of David Raya, but the news around the Arsenal number 1 was a little more positive than expected. In his press conference yesterday, Mikel Arteta said:.

It has been revealed that he’s not fit for tomorrow, unfortunately, but it doesn’t look too serious. We need some more tests tomorrow, but it’s quite encouraging. With the pain that he was showing immediately after the action, we were all quite worried, but he seems to be better than what we expected.

Sources indicate that we expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain that he had at that moment, and the first test that we’ve done revealed something that is much more encouraging. There’s no need for surgery, which was the main fear especially because that would rule him out for months, so let’s see.

So, it seems like he’s going to miss a few games, but not anything prolonged, which is obviously good news. Elsewhere, there’s room for rotation, and I think this might be a good chance to give minutes to William Saliba who hasn’t played competitively since the World Cup. He’s had a couple of behind closed doors appearances, which will be useful in terms of fitness, but nothing compares with actually playing at this level.

I wonder too if players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will fancy their chances, but that seems like a lot of change in the back four – and the goalkeeper – so we’ll have to wait and see there. In midfield, we can bring Myles Lewis-Skelly in for a start, but obviously the manager has plenty to choose from in there, and up front I imagine it will be a chance for Viktor Gyokeres whose minutes have been scant so far this season. Asked if the striker had been knocking on his door about that, Arteta mentioned:.

No, we have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing, to gather information about the way they are feeling, and so far, it’s been very positive with Viktor and with the rest of the team.

He could really use a goal tonight if he does start, as does Christos Tzolis whose numbers so far this season aren’t where you’d like them to be. Obviously there’s more to assessing a player than simply goals and assists, but for a left winger brought into replace two players who contributed a lot to the team over the last few seasons, just two assists from 11 appearances (Community Shield excluded) is a little below what you’d hope. He has had an injury, of course, but if his season needs a kick-start, tonight would be very timely.

Dortmund sit top of the Bundesliga right now, unbeaten in the league thus far, and with just one defeat all season in all competitions. That did come in the Champions League, away to Bodo Glimt, but this will be a tricky test tonight for Arsenal. Arteta says:.

It has been revealed that I’m very impressed with them, you see the results so far, where they are in the Bundesliga at the top and where they are in the Champions League and especially the way they are playing, the way they are dominating games, the amount of threat they are able to create. We had them here in pre-season, and they revealed the quality and what they are capable of, so we are very much aware of that. But we play at home in front of our crowd, and now we’re going to go and attack the game, that’s for sure.

Recent findings suggest that after a disappointing second half against Newcastle on Saturday, I’m sure the manager will be looking for a response from his side. It’s nice to be at home again, and a long spell of games in London will hopefully less taxing physically without all the travel, so it’d be good to get that off to a winning start tonight.

Elsewhere, Bruno Guimaraes spoke about his first few months at the club, and how he now feels like he’s getting to grips with what Mikel Arteta wants from him, saying:.

It has been revealed that I’m here, I don’t know, three, four months? It’s still a lot to go, but I now definitely understand my role in the team, the way that Mikel wants me to play in the team. So, yeah, I think I still can play much, much better.

And it’s quite interesting to hear him talk about how at Arsenal he is more ‘free’ than he was under Eddie Howe at Newcastle. Most would feel it was the other way around, but he explained:.

Industry observers note that it’s very different. When I was at Newcastle, you play more positional, keep more your position. Here it’s a little bit more free.

If you see the game against Newcastle, they were marking us man to man. You see JT [Jurrien Timber] plays a six, an eight and a number nine sometimes, so you have to move a lot. Of course, I was not used to it. So now I understand a little bit more what he wants for the midfield.

I think there’s more to come from him, he’s looked good at times, a little off the pace at others, and I think my main worry is about the physical side of his game. Does he have the running power and athleticism that enables players like Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard to thrive under this manager? At 29, he’s no spring chicken, but I guess there’s always room for improvement. Anyway, his press conference stuff from yesterday is worth reading, and there’s some good chat about him on the Arsecast Extra which you’ll find below.

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Recent findings suggest that tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending looks and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and Fresh Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

Sources indicate that "Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in.".

An crucial game at the bottom end of the League One table will take place at the Cherry Red Records Stadium on Saturday, as AFC Wimbledon welcome Barnsley.

The hosts sit 18th but only lead the drop zone by three points while their visitors are rooted to the foot of the division and in the midst of a losing run.

AFC Wimbledon are back in League One action on Saturday in search of a second straight home victory to extend their lead over the relegation zone.

The Dons enjoyed a positive start to their second straight campaign in the third tier, earning 12 points from their first eight outings, but they were swiftly dragged towards the bottom end of the division, losing four and drawing one of the next five matches.

They scored just three goals in those matches and right now have a league-low tally of 11 goals from 18 games, albeit they were able to make a crucial return to winning ways at home to Blackpool in mid-November, as Alistair Smith's early goal made the only difference.

Johnnie Jackson's men were unable to build on that last time out, though, visiting Leyton Orient and losing 4-1 having trailed by three at the break and pulled one back through Harry Cornick only for Alex Gilbert to put the game out of sight 20 minutes from time.

Now sat 18th, just three points and two places above the bottom four, and with just one league win on the board since mid-September, AFC Wimbledon will again bid to bounce back on Saturday and move further clear of the drop zone and towards mid-table.

Their visitors, meanwhile, head south aiming to arrest a bigger slump which has seen them cut adrift at the bottom of the table.

Daniel Stendel's return to the Barnsley dugout for the 2026-27 season has not gone to blueprint thus far, as the Yorkshire outfit sit bottom of League One on just nine points from 15 games having won just two and lost 10 of those.

One of those wins and six defeats have come from the Reds' eight away league games thus far, conceding 16 goals in those, while Stendel's men are winless in 11 third-tier outings since early September including three straight defeats heading into the weekend and seven in their last eight.

Following 2-1 losses to Wigan Athletic and South Yorkshire rivals Sheffield Wednesday, they visited Bradford City on Tuesday and suffered a 3-0 beating as Stephen Humphrys scored a brace and Jake Beesley added a late third.

Now rooted to the bottom of the league, four points behind the four teams above them, Barnsley will be desperate to end their long wait for a victory on Saturday and begin climbing towards safety after their dismal start.

Barnsley form (all competitions):.

AFC Wimbledon remain without forward Mathew Stevens due to a long-term injury, while Dujuan Richards and Dan Sweeney are also sidelined.

Attacker Jayden Stockley is back in contention, though, after a suspension last time out, and he will return up front having scored six of the Dons' 11 league goals so far this season.

Cornick will hope to join him, having scored in Stockley's absence at the weekend, with Miles Hippolyte also hoping to continue in an attacking role.

Barnsley are unable to call on attackers Amani Richards, Fabio Jalo and Tobi Adeyemo on Saturday.

Stendel may make changes from the midweek 3-0 loss, with Jubril Okedina in line to return to the defence and Daniel Johnson an option to join Luca Connell in midfield.

That would allow top scorer and captain Cameron McGeehan to return to an advanced midfield role, where he, Reyes Cleary and Vimal Yoganathan may support a lone striker.

AFC Wimbledon possible starting lineup:.

Bishop; Sessegnon, Ogundere, Johnson, Seddon; Nelson, Maycock, Browne; Cornick, Stockley, Hippolyte.

Barnsley possible starting lineup:.

Slicker; Okedina, Kay, Gale, Larkeche; Johnson, Connell; Yoganathan, McGeehan, Cleary; Kirk.

Both teams will see Saturday's game as a significant opportunity to begin turning their form around and it could be a crucial one between the division's worst attack and its second-worst defence and most out-of-form team.

Barnsley look totally devoid of confidence, though, while AFC Wimbledon were able to get the better of Blackpool when they last met fellow strugglers, making them favourites with the best football betting sites, and we give an edge to the hosts as a result.

Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering.
  • Recent findings suggest that A long-standing challenge in genome engineering is how to achieve precise, programmable integration of large (≥1 kb) DNA cargo.
  • It has been revealed that a, Transposon organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering. CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs)1,2 offer a promising solution by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration. Because of their exceptional targeting fidelity, type I-F3 CASTs have been a major research focus1, yet the structural basis of their RNA-guided DNA integration has remained unclear. Here, using cryo-electron microscopy, computational protein design and functional assays, we report the licensing mechanisms that control DNA integration activity of Vibrio cholerae CAST (VchCAST). Structural determination was enabled by zero-shot computational redesign of TnsA, which enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude without compromising specificity. The structure of the holo integration complex reveals the conformational licensing events that govern activation of the integration machinery at the on-target site. Multiple components (Cascade–TniQ, TnsC and TnsA–TnsB) undergo conformational changes upon assembly into the holo integration complex, and the catalytically competent state is stabilized only within the full assembly. Comparison with existing CAST integration complex structures reveals conserved architectural features, suggesting a common molecular basis for RNA-guided transposition across CASTs. Our findings establish a general mechanistic framework for RNA-guided DNA integration and demonstrate that protein design is a powerful strategy for engineering highly active CAST systems.

Recent findings suggest that A long-standing challenge in genome engineering is how to achieve precise, programmable integration of large (≥1 kb) DNA cargo. CRISPR–Cas nucleases are capable of efficient DNA cleavage3, but their reliance on host DNA repair pathways limits both the efficiency and fidelity of large insertions4. CASTs offer an alternative strategy by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration, without the need for DNA double-strand breaks or homologous recombination1,2. CASTs evolved from Tn7-like transposons through the acquisition of a CRISPR effector, with distinct effectors defining each of the major subfamilies: type V-K, I-F3, I-B and I-D5. All CASTs encode a conserved set of proteins: TniQ (bridging protein), TnsC (AAA+ regulator) and TnsA–TnsB (TnsA/B, transposase complex) (Fig. 1a). The CRISPR effector and TniQ form the targeting module, and TnsA/B and TnsC form the transposition machinery (Fig. 1a). Although all CASTs perform RNA-guided transposition, they can display a remarkable diversity of targeting behaviours. For example, in type I-B2 CASTs, the transposition machinery can associate with either the sequence-specific DNA-binding protein TnsD or an RNA-guided targeting complex6. Type V-K CASTs exhibit a robust off-target pathway, driven by the propensity of TniQ and TnsC to load at non-cognate sites7. Type I-F3 CASTs have a Cascade effector and exhibit near-exclusive on-target integration8, which makes them of particular interest for clinical9 and microbial genome-editing applications10.

It has been revealed that a, Transposon organization. R and L, right and left transposon ends. Parallel lines indicate discontinuity. b, Dual screen of TnsA designs: activity and specificity scores are plotted relative to wild type (normalized to 0,0), with density plots on the top and right. The red circle represents the top design, D1A. c, In vivo integration activity of VchCAST. The graph reveals individual data points. Data are mean ± s.d. from biological triplicates. Ara, arabinose selection; Kan, kanamycin selection. d, In vivo genome-wide insertion profile. Red arrow indicates target site. e, Close-up view of target site in d with insertion window. f, Cryo-EM density map (2.9 Å) of the class 1 STC at 0.129 threshold. Proteins coloured as in a. Target-site duplication is shown in red. g, Top, atomic model of the STC oriented as in f. Black symbols (asterisk, star and diamond) indicate regions shown in h–k. Bottom, domain organization of TnsB. Striped regions represent disordered N- and C-terminal tails. CD, catalytic domain; DBD, DNA-binding domain. h, Overlay of the catalytic TnsB in STC assembly class 2 (white) and class 1 (purple) shows conformational changes involved in transition from class 2 to class 1, with the catalytic domain and TBD rotating as indicated. View rotated 90° relative to g. i, Class 2 model shown in the same orientation as in g. Catalytic residues D223, D308 and E344 are shown as sticks; dashed lines indicate unresolved positions (331–341). j, Same as i, for the class 1 model. Magnesium ions are shown as green spheres. k, Close-up view of the region marked by the diamond and asterisk in g, rotated by 10°.

Recent findings suggest that recent structural studies of CAST assemblies have begun to reveal how this conserved transposition machinery accommodates architecturally diverse CRISPR effectors. The V-K system from Scytonema hofmannii, ShCAST, is the best characterized to date; its holo integration complex (HIC) structure shows that the host factor S15 and TniQ associate with Cas12k and together strongly distort target DNA, an event that is required to recruit two helical turns of hexameric TnsC11,12, which in turn engages the transposase TnsB via its C-terminal hook13. A complete TnsABCD integration complex structure exists for type I-B2 CAST14, but structural information on other CAST assemblies is limited to isolated components or subcomplexes. TnsC organization is not fixed across CAST systems, as it forms a heptameric ring in other CAST systems, including I-F315 and I-B216, as well as in Tn717. Whether mechanistic insights from one system can be extended to other CAST systems is unclear.

Despite extensive biochemical, genetic and structural studies of individual components, the mechanisms by which type I-F3 CASTs achieve precise on-target integration remain unknown. Chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) experiments have revealed a hierarchical assembly pathway in which Cascade–TniQ occupancy precedes TnsC recruitment, and stable TnsC accumulation depends on the transposase TnsA/B15. Cascade–TniQ binds DNA promiscuously and forms partial R-loops at many candidate sites15, but they cannot complete R-loop formation on their own18, suggesting that additional steps are required to license TnsC recruitment. Structures of TnsC15 have established the molecular details of its homo-oligomerization on DNA. Nonetheless, how all these components come together to form an integration-competent complex at the RNA-guided target site remains unknown. Thus, a structure of the fully assembled HIC is critical to establish the mechanistic basis for RNA-guided DNA integration and for rational engineering efforts to improve type I-F3 CAST integration efficiency for translational applications9,19.

Industry observers note that here, using a combination of computational protein design, single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and directed in vivo mutagenesis, we uncover the mechanisms that regulate HIC assembly in the type I-F3 VchCAST system. The architectures of the strand-transfer complex (STC) and the full HIC reveal how RNA-guided target recognition, TnsC oligomerization and TnsA/B recruitment converge to organize a stable integration complex. Despite large structural differences across type V-K, I-F3 and I-B2 CASTs, conserved local features suggest universal mechanistic principles of RNA-guided DNA integration across CASTs. Our results reveal a context-dependent structural mechanism, whereby each of the aforementioned components undergoes significant conformational rearrangements relative to their isolated structures15,18,20 as a means to license RNA-guided integration complex assembly. Our work also demonstrates how structure-guided computational protein design can be leveraged as a highly effective strategy for improving integration activity without compromising specificity.

Because TnsA was refractory to purification (Methods), we hypothesized that stabilizing it in a product-bound conformation could both enhance activity and facilitate structure determination. We therefore modelled the VchCAST STC (comprising TnsA, TnsB and a strand-transfer DNA substrate) using AlphaFold 321 (Extended Data Fig. 1). We then redesigned the TnsA sequence using LigandMPNN22, with functionally notable residues held fixed (32%; 74 out of 230 residues; Supplementary Fig. 1) and applied per-residue sampling biased towards TnsA homologues. Designs were grouped by sequence divergence from wild-type TnsA (TnsAWT), then selected for experimental screening on the basis of predicted confidence scores (Methods).

We screened 500 top-ranking designs, each containing between 2 and 87 substitutions (Supplementary Table 1), using our previously developed high-throughput Escherichia coli screen23. In brief, a kanamycin resistance cassette serves as the donor DNA, such that kanamycin selection reports overall integration activity. On-target genomic integration is enriched by dual kanamycin and arabinose selection, which selects for disruption of an arabinose-inducible ccdB toxin gene. Activity and specificity scores are calculated as the log2-transformed fold change in variant frequency compared to wild type23. Of the 500 designs tested, 67% demonstrated higher activity than TnsAWT (Fig. 1b). The top-performing design (D1A; Fig. 1b) incorporates 27 mutations (Extended Data Fig. 2) and has a log2-transformed activity score of 6.37, with no significant change in specificity (specificity score = −0.27; Fig. 1b). This improvement translates in vivo to an approximately 100-fold increase in integration activity relative to TnsAWT (Fig. 1c) while maintaining high fidelity, with 98% of insertions occurring on target (Fig. 1d) and at the expected distance, 82 base pairs (bp) from the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM)1 (Fig. 1e).

TnsA is required for transposition, but its catalytic activity determines product identity: cleavage of the 5′ donor end generates simple insertions, whereas a failure to cleave generates co-integrates24. Long-read sequencing distinguishes these two products, establishing the extent of TnsA activity8. Using long-read sequencing, we found that D1A produced more co-integrates than wild-type TnsA (42% simple insertions versus 96.2%; Extended Data Fig. 3). This phenotype was attributable primarily to the Q73K substitution: reverting Q73 to the wild-type residue restored simple insertion frequency to near wild-type levels (92.4%) without compromising the transposition activity gains conferred by the broader D1A redesign (Extended Data Fig. 3), indicating that Q73K governs the simple insertion/co-integrate balance independently of those gains. This also does not appear to be a general consequence of the design campaign, as other top-scoring designs retain full catalytic activity (97–100% simple insertions; Extended Data Fig. 3). Finally, we examined the effect of redesign on the folded state of TnsA. Circular dichroism analysis revealed that TnsAWT has substantial random coil content, consistent with an unfolded protein, whereas D1A has a spectrum consistent with a well-folded, mostly α-helical protein (Supplementary Fig. 2). Together, these results demonstrate that zero-shot structure-based computational design can both improve CAST activity and facilitate structure determination, creating a framework for iterative structure-guided optimization.

Recent findings suggest that we next determined the cryo-EM structure of the STC containing integration host factor (IHF), D1A (hereafter referred to as TnsA), TnsB and a strand-transfer DNA substrate (2.9 Å overall resolution; Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4). We found that K73 occupies a second-shell position relative to the TnsA active site, sufficiently close to form a hydrogen bond with catalytic residues, providing a likely explanation for why the Q73K substitution reduces the catalytic activity of TnsA (Supplementary Fig. 5). As this perturbation is confined to the local active site environment, the D1A structure presented here should therefore represent an otherwise catalytically competent state. IHF promotes CAST transposition 10-fold, although it is not absolutely required for activity25. In our structure, IHF binds LE DNA at a site between LE1 and LE2 (Supplementary Fig. 3), bending the DNA to permit occupancy of additional TnsB binding sites. This binding mode has been described in molecular detail in a related study that lacked TnsA and other components of the HIC20. Here, we instead focus on the novel insights we observe in the presence of the partner protein TnsA.

It has been revealed that tnsA localizes to the 5′ end of the donor DNA, where it binds the flanking host DNA and forms a continuous β-sheet with TnsB, a feature highly similar to previous TnsA structures from the type I-B2 PmcCAST system (Supplementary Fig. 6). We also identified conformational flexibility in the STC ensemble, which was separable by 3D classification. The highest-resolution class, containing the majority of particles, corresponds to class 1 (Supplementary Fig. 7a), whereas a second, minor 3D class (27% of particles, 3.2 Å overall resolution) lacks observable density for target DNA and for TnsB beyond the C-terminal helix (CTH) domain (class 2; Supplementary Fig. 7b,c and Extended Data Table 1). Closer inspection of class 2 reveals that the catalytic DDE triad (D223, D308, and E344) is too distant (6.2–6.9 Å; Supplementary Fig. 8) to form a functional active site, and that the loop preceding E344 (residues 331–341) is disordered (Fig. 1i). By contrast, class 1 has the expected arrangement of catalytic residues, as well as two magnesium ions: a catalytic magnesium with the expected coordination geometry and a second structural magnesium positioned nearby that stabilizes a sharp bend at the target–donor DNA junction (Fig. 1j). The conformational transition from class 2 to class 1 would entail a ~20° rotation of the catalytic domain and target DNA-binding domain (TBD) of TnsB at the TnsA–TnsB interface (blue star, Fig. 1h), reorienting these domains to engage target DNA. Concurrently, a target DNA-binding loop in the catalytic domain of TnsB (residues 359–378) becomes structured, further priming the complex for target DNA binding (Fig. 1k). These structural observations show that the STC exhibits conformational heterogeneity; one conformation (class 2) appearing catalytically inactive, and the other (class 1) showing rearrangements consistent with active site organization and target DNA engagement. As TnsA/B requires additional transposon-encoded partner proteins (that is, TnsC) for integration activity1, these conformational changes may reflect a mechanism of activation for TnsA/B.

We next determined the cryo-EM structure of the HIC, comprising Cascade–TniQ, TnsA, TnsB and TnsC, assembled on a strand-transfer DNA substrate that mimics the in vivo integration product (Supplementary Fig. 3). Our cryo-EM data analysis reveals substantial compositional heterogeneity, with three identifiable assemblies (Extended Data Fig. 4): Cascade–TniQ (target-recognition complex (TRC); 3 Å overall resolution), STC–TnsC (4.3 Å overall resolution) and the HIC (4.5 Å overall resolution; Fig. 2a). In the HIC, local resolution is highest at the Cascade core (3.7 Å) and decreases towards the STC periphery (about 7 Å; Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Although IHF was included in the reconstitution, we did not observe IHF bound in the resulting structure, which may be attributable to the sample preparation method (Methods). Notably, the overall map was of sufficient quality to interpret different structural features without the need of a composite map stitched from subtracted focused-refined regions.

It has been revealed that the HIC contains a Cascade effector, a TniQ dimer, a heptameric TnsC ring, a TnsB tetramer and two copies of TnsA (Fig. 2b), consistent with the stoichiometry established by structures of individual subcomplexes15,18,20. However, density for the seventh TnsC protomer (TnsC7) is noticeably weaker than for the other subunits (Supplementary Fig. 10), indicating substoichiometric occupancy or flexibility. The DNA-binding footprint accounts for the characteristic 82 bp integration distance from the PAM: 32 nucleotides occupied by the guide RNA spacer, followed by a 21, 14 and 15 bp footprint corresponding to TniQ, TnsC and TnsB, respectively, and terminating in a 5-nucleotide target-site duplication (Fig. 2c). Mutagenesis of the Cas8/5 PAM-interacting residues S127, R243, N246 and D461 substantially reduces integration activity (Supplementary Fig. 11), consistent with an crucial role for these residues in PAM recognition and transposition. Our structure of the VchCAST HIC reveals an arrangement wherein TnsC acts as a bifunctional adaptor, interacting with TniQ via its N-terminal face and with the STC via its C-terminal face (Fig. 2b). This architectural role of TnsC is similar to previous observations in ShCAST (type V-K)12 and PmcCAST (type I-B2) systems14,16. This modularity explains how CAST systems have diversified to co-opt a wide range of CRISPR effectors while preserving the core transposition mechanism.

It has been revealed that A central question is how the targeting module is physically coupled to the core transposition machinery. In the HIC, TniQ2 serves as the primary physical bridge between the target recognition and transposition machinery (Fig. 3a), forming a predominantly hydrophobic interface with TnsC1 (Fig. 3b). Consistent with the functional importance of this interface, alanine substitutions at F2, L3 and F40 substantially reduced integration activity (Fig. 3c). TniQ forms a constitutive homodimer, but only the TniQ2 monomer interacts with TnsC, mirroring observations in the evolutionarily distant ShCAST and PmcCAST, in which a single TniQ subunit recruits TnsC12,16. Remarkably, despite the divergent overall architectures of the ShCAST (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8EA3), PmcCAST (PDB: 8FF4) and VchCAST integration complexes, the TniQ–TnsC interface is notably conserved (Extended Data Fig. 5). In particular, the TnsC finger loop, previously shown to mediate critical TniQ interactions in ShCAST12, engages TniQ2 similarly in VchCAST (Extended Data Fig. 5). Consistent with this observation, truncations within the TnsC finger loop severely reduce transposition activity15. These findings identify the TniQ–TnsC interface as a shared docking point that may enable architecturally diverse CRISPR effectors to couple to common transposition machinery.

Industry observers note that tnsB activity is strictly dependent on TnsC-mediated recruitment to the target site15, making these interactions central to understanding integration. We next examined how TnsB engages TnsC within the HIC, revealing multiple points of contact along the C-terminal face of TnsC, specifically at protomers TnsC2, TnsC3 and TnsC6 (Fig. 3d). Notably, the TBD of TnsB localizes to the TnsC2–TnsC3 interface (Fig. 3e), consistent with previous ShCAST and PmcCAST structures12,14 (Extended Data Fig. 6). Across Tn7-like transposons, ATP binding, but not hydrolysis, is required for integration activity26,27. AAA+ initiator clade regulators require ATP for oligomerization, as the ATP-binding pocket is formed at the inter-protomer interface28. This implies that transposition requires TnsC oligomerization on target DNA, although the mechanistic basis for this requirement has remained unclear. The conserved interaction between the TBD of TnsB and the TnsC inter-protomer interface now suggests that TnsB directly senses the oligomeric state of TnsC, providing a structural explanation for this long-standing observation.

It has been revealed that another conserved feature across CAST systems is the interaction between TnsC and the extreme C terminus of TnsB, known as the hook, which is critical for transposition13. The interchangeability of TnsB hooks between type I-F3 CASTs29 underscores the importance of these structured interactions within otherwise disordered regions. Consistent with this role, we observe continuous density connecting the CTH (residues 563–573) of TnsB to the surface of TnsC6 (Fig. 3f), although additional contacts are likely to remain undetected owing to the length and extensive disorder of this region. The TnsB hook is predicted by AlphaFold 321 to correspond to the last eight residues of TnsB, an assignment supported by cryo-EM density observed in the HIC (Extended Data Fig. 7). The hook binding site in VchTnsC aligns well with ShTnsC13 and PmcTnsC14 (Extended Data Fig. 7), indicating that although structural details may differ, the binding location is conserved.

Having identified the TnsB hook interaction with TnsC, we reasoned that the disordered N- and C-terminal regions in all components of the core transposition machinery (TnsABC; Supplementary Fig. 12) could mediate additional interactions. Consistent with this idea, we observed contacts between the N terminus of TnsB and TnsA, and between the C-terminal tail of TnsC and TnsB (Fig. 3g). Residues 3–10 of the disordered N terminus of TnsB occupy a hydrophobic pocket on TnsA (Fig. 3h) close to aromatic residues F6 and F9, consistent with AlphaFold 3 predictions21 (Extended Data Fig. 1) and sequence conservation analysis (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Although N-terminal truncation (Δ1–10) caused a significant reduction in transposition activity, the TnsB F9A mutation reproduced almost none of this effect, suggesting that residues other than F9 mediate the relevant contacts within the truncated region (Extended Data Fig. 8c). The C-terminal tail of TnsC (residues 321–330) is positioned against the CTH of TnsB (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 8b) at a hydrophobic interface, also supported by AlphaFold 3 predictions21 (Supplementary Fig. 13) and conservation analysis (Extended Data Fig. 8b). The TnsC F329A mutation almost fully abrogated transposition activity, similar to the effect of C-terminal truncation of TnsC (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Analogous interactions between the C terminus of TnsC and the STC occur in PmcCAST, albeit involving different subunits and interfaces14 (Extended Data Fig. 9). These findings uncover a previously unrecognized network of interactions involving the unstructured termini of TnsA, TnsB and TnsC, revealing how the core transposition machinery may maintain associations to facilitate integration-competent assembly.

A previous cryo-EM structure of VchTnsC solved in the presence of DNA revealed an open heptameric ring-like arrangement in which the bound DNA was poorly resolved (PDB: 7UFI)15. In our HIC structure, although we clearly resolved the path of target DNA, no specific TnsC–DNA interactions could be precisely mapped. Thus, it is likely that the TnsC ring primarily associates with target DNA via the complementary basic surface formed by its central pore (Supplementary Fig. 14). This is consistent with previous data showing that TnsC binds DNA relatively weakly15, suggesting that TnsC requires partner proteins such as TniQ to initiate oligomerization on target DNA. Notably, comparison with PDB 7UFI reveals that the heptameric ring is significantly more open in the HIC. Aligning on TnsC1 results in an 11 Å displacement at TnsC7 relative to the equivalent protomer in PDB 7UFI (Fig. 3j), the result of an average 0.8 Å greater rise per protomer (Supplementary Fig. 15). This indicates that partner proteins induce larger conformational changes than those observed in TnsC with DNA alone. Our observations suggest that the oligomeric state of TnsC is sensitive to the presence of the partner proteins TniQ and TnsB and is mediated through distinct interaction interfaces located on specific TnsC protomers.

We next investigated how TnsC is selectively recruited to the target site. The compositional heterogeneity of our reconstitution enabled us to resolve a free Cascade–TniQ complex (Extended Data Fig. 4) (TRC; 3.0 Å overall resolution; Fig. 4a) that closely resembles a prior structure of the target DNA-bound VchCAST Cascade–TniQ complex18 (Supplementary Fig. 16). This previously reported structure featured a partial R-loop and a disordered Cas8/5 helical bundle domain (HBD)18. By contrast, the Cascade–TniQ complex in the HIC (Fig. 4b) adopts a fully engaged conformation characterized by a complete R-loop and a structured Cas8/5 HBD. Comparison of Cascade–TniQ in the TRC and HIC structures reveals that R-loop completion is accompanied by a conformational change in TniQ2 to engage both target DNA and TnsC (Extended Data Fig. 10).

Industry observers note that the non-target genomic strand (NTGS) is threaded through an electropositive channel at the tripartite TniQ1–TniQ2–Cas8/5 HBD interface, where it rejoins the target genomic strand (TGS) to reform the target DNA duplex downstream of the R-loop junction (Fig. 4c,d). The Cas8/5 HBD contributes to this channel through electrostatic contacts with the NTGS via R310, R311, K314 and R370 (Supplementary Fig. 17). Additionally, a previously uncharacterized loop within the Cas8/5 HBD (residues KSLIPEN), which we term the TniQ-interacting loop (TIL), interacts directly with TniQ1 (Fig. 4e). The functional importance of this interface is confirmed by alanine substitutions in the Cas8/5 HBD, TIL and at TniQ1 residues D361, S358 and W394, all of which substantially reduce integration activity (Figs. 3c and 4f).

Sources indicate that separately, TniQ2 engages target DNA through two distinct modes: hydrophobic packing against the R-loop junction (L326, L336, V362 and T363; Fig. 4g) and electrostatic interactions with the DNA backbone via basic and polar residues (R58, K65, R71, S104 and S106; Fig. 4h,i). Mutagenesis of residues at both interfaces substantially reduces integration activity, consistent with their functional importance (Fig. 3c). These observations establish that R-loop completion drives a conformational transition in the target recognition module that repositions TniQ to engage target DNA and license recruitment of the core transposition machinery.

In a recent development, we propose the following working model for RNA-guided transposition, based on our findings and incorporating prior observations on CASTs and other Tn7-like systems. Cascade–TniQ promiscuously samples genomic locations15, consistent with its ability to stably bind target DNA with only partial R-loop formation (Fig. 5). A cooperative conformational rearrangement in Cas8/5 and TniQ is required to stabilize the full R-loop and enable TnsC recruitment, with direct contacts of TniQ at the R-loop junction providing a structural readout of R-loop completion. This coupling is further supported by molecular dynamics simulations demonstrating correlated motions between Cas8/5 and TniQ30. We observe no other DNA distortions consistent with specific recognition of the target site by the transposon-encoded machinery (Supplementary Fig. 18), contrary to that observed in other Tn7-like systems14,31. Further insight into target-site selectivity comes from the observation that PAM-distal mismatches permit Cascade binding but abolish transposition15. The conformational rearrangements in the HIC occur near spacer nucleotide positions 25–32, raising the possibility that mismatches in this region could introduce geometric incompatibility that prevents stable docking of the HBD and subsequent TnsC recruitment (Fig. 5). TnsC oligomerization is required to recruit TnsA/B to the target site and may be sensed directly by TnsB through conserved interactions spanning TnsC protomers. Whether full heptamer formation is required prior to TnsA/B recruitment remains unknown and is not resolvable using our reconstitution approach; however, previous work on Tn7 suggests that oligomerization is completed prior to TnsA/B recruitment32.

Major licensing events during RNA-guided DNA integration directly at the CRISPR effector (a) and at the transposase (b). a, Top left, the TRC (PDB: 36BQ) displays an unstructured Cas8/5 helical bundle domain, a partial R-loop and an outward-open TniQ conformation. Unstructured regions are indicated with dotted lines. This state can sample many genomic locations (dotted arrows) in addition to the programmed target site (red box). Top right, upon recognition of the target, the TRC forms stabilizing interactions between Cas8/5 and TniQ, promoting R-loop completion and enabling recruitment of TnsC to complete this licensing step (lock symbol). Middle, off-target complexes (grey) are unable to form a complete R-loop (red X) and the Cas8/5 helical bundle domain remains flexible, and TnsC cannot be recruited. b, Top left, the TnsB-only STC (PDB: 9Y7B) contains flexible target-binding domains and an incompletely arranged active site, shown inside the white circle as a disconnected DDE catalytic triad. Top right and middle, upon addition of TnsA, the TnsA/B STC adopts two conformational states that exist in equilibrium: class 2 (PDB: 36BP) and class 1 (PDB: 36BO). The class 1 state exhibits the catalytically competent arrangement of the DDE triad (triangle within the circle). Dotted lines indicate flexible connections between components, including the interface between TnsA and TnsB. The targeting module (orange) and transposition module (purple) assemble with TnsC to form the HIC (PDB: 36AU). Both the targeting and the transposition modules adopt stable conformations and are locked into an integration-competent conformation. The DDE triad forms a catalytically competent active site. The C-terminal tails of TnsB and TnsC function to loosely couple components, with the hook of TnsB inserting into a TnsC pocket, forming β-sheet interactions (purple arrow), while the TnsC C-terminal tail contacts TnsB near target DNA. Dotted lines indicate disordered regions.

Industry observers note that tnsB also undergoes multiple layers of activation through association with partner proteins TnsA and TnsC. In isolation, the DDE catalytic triad is improperly arranged and too distant to coordinate magnesium ion binding, and target DNA remains disordered even when a strand-transfer substrate is provided20. Association with TnsA is insufficient to fully stabilize the catalytically competent conformation (Fig. 5). Only in the context of the HIC, in which both TnsA and TnsC are present, are the catalytic residues locked into an integration-competent state and target DNA stably accommodated. Although our reliance on a strand-transfer substrate does not allow us to establish the stepwise order of these conformations directly, the inactive-to-active transition that we observe is, to our knowledge, unreported in CAST systems despite extensive structural work from our group and others13,14,33. Notably, a conceptually related precedent exists in IS21, where the transposase IstA transitions from an inactive to an active conformation upon association with its obligate AAA+ partner IstB34, suggesting that conformational licensing may be an effective mechanism for ensuring selective activation of integration across Tn7 and related transposons. In summary, we propose that each component of the integration machinery undergoes conformational changes upon incorporation into the HIC, providing a structural basis for the exceptionally high on-target specificity characteristic of type I-F3 CAST systems. Both the targeting module Cascade–TniQ and the transposase TnsA/B serve to license RNA-guided DNA integration, ensuring that catalytic competence is only achieved upon assembly of the complete machinery at the RNA-guided target site.

Structured interactions embedded within intrinsically disordered regions of CAST proteins have critical roles in transposition, most notably through the C-terminal hook of TnsB12,29. Here, combining our cryo-EM structure with AlphaFold 3 predictions, we localize the C-terminal hook of TnsB and identify its binding site on TnsC. We also identify two previously unrecognized interactions: the N terminus of TnsB engages a pocket on TnsA, and the C terminus of TnsC contacts TnsB in close proximity to target DNA. These findings reveal an extensive network of structured interactions within otherwise disordered termini that physically connect the core transposition machinery prior to integration complex assembly. The mapping of these contacts has direct implications for the rational engineering of chimeric CAST systems and the design of improved variants.

According to recent reports, the structural characterization of CAST systems has been largely motivated by the goal of engineering more efficient tools for genome editing; however, structure-guided efforts to improve CAST activity have had limited success29,35,36. Here we demonstrate that a high-throughput structure-based design approach can overcome these limitations, presenting a compelling and scalable alternative to directed evolution. We propose that thermodynamic stabilization of the integration-competent conformation is key to improve activity. This is consistent with the thermodynamic requirements of cut-and-paste transposition: the chemically isoenergetic reaction proceeds through states of increasing stability, and the product complex can be so stable that unfoldases (for example, ClpX) are required for its disassembly in vivo37. Consistent with this hypothesis, zero-shot structure-based protein design of a single protein, TnsA, enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude in E. coli, approaching the gains achieved through seven rounds of directed evolution applied across the entire PseCAST system19. Notably, the redesigned variant not only improved integration activity but also enabled structural characterization of the HIC, illustrating how computational design and structural biology can be synergistic approaches.

The compromised catalytic activity of the top design variant D1A is attributable primarily to a lysine substitution at position 73, which is within range to form hydrogen-bonding interactions with the catalytic residue D91. We hypothesized that this substitution directly perturbs active site chemistry, which motivated our prioritization of the reversion mutant for testing; consistent with this hypothesis, reversion almost fully restored catalytic activity while maintaining substantial increases in activity. This trade-off reflects a known limitation of structure-based design methods: approaches such as ProteinMPNN can inadvertently stabilize protein structure at the expense of catalytic function38, as functional residues are often locally destabilizing to the protein fold39. Therefore, success of the design strategy proposed here depends on mechanistic knowledge and the availability of a high-quality model of the integration-competent complex, precisely what the structures presented here provide, and what has been lacking in previous engineering efforts.

The codon-optimized gene encoding VchTnsB from V. cholerae Tn6677 was subcloned into the pARZ4 expression vector carrying a carbenicillin resistance marker, which was engineered to append an N-terminal hexahistidine (His6) tag followed by a maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag and a TEV protease recognition site. The sequence-verified construct was introduced into One Shot BL21(DE3) chemically competent E. coli cells (Invitrogen) for recombinant production.

Expression cultures were grown in 2× YT medium supplemented with 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin at 37 °C with shaking until OD600 reached 0.4–0.6. Protein expression was induced by the addition of 0.25 mM isopropyl-β-d-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG), and cultures were subsequently incubated overnight at 16 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C and resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% NP-40, 1 mM DTT, and protease inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific; one tablet per 30 ml). Cells were lysed by probe sonication on ice using alternating 5 s on–10 s off cycles, and insoluble debris was removed by centrifugation at 16,000 rpm for 30 min at 4 °C.

Recent findings suggest that the clarified lysate was applied to an amylose affinity column (Fresh England Biolabs) pre-equilibrated with wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT). The resin was washed with 15–20 column volumes of wash buffer to remove non-specifically bound proteins, and the MBP–VchTnsB fusion was eluted by supplementing the wash buffer with 10 mM maltose. Peak fractions were pooled and diluted to 200 mM NaCl using heparin dilution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol) before loading onto a HiTrap Heparin HP column (Cytiva) on an ÄKTA Pure FPLC system. Bound protein was eluted over a linear NaCl gradient from 200 mM to 1.1 M in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4) and 5% glycerol buffer. Peak fractions were resolved by size-exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 column (GE Healthcare) equilibrated in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl, and 5% glycerol. Purity was assessed by Coomassie-stained SDS–PAGE, and purified fractions were aliquoted, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C.

For applications requiring tag-free VchTnsB, an alternative construct was generated by engineering a SUMO–Ulp protease cleavage cassette between the His6–MBP tag and the VchTnsB coding sequence. Expression and amylose affinity purification were performed as detailed above. Post elution, the pooled fractions were subjected to overnight Ulp1 protease digestion at 4 °C (1 mg protease per 50–100 mg of target protein) to remove the affinity tag, followed by the same downstream heparin affinity and size-exclusion chromatography workflow under identical buffer conditions.

Industry observers note that cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 30 min at 4 °C and resuspended in Strep lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 0.1% NP-40, 1 mM DTT, and protease inhibitor cocktail (1 tablet per 30 ml). Recent findings suggest that eluted fractions were pooled and subjected to overnight digestion at 4 °C with Ulp1 protease at an approximate 1:100 enzyme-to-protein mass ratio to remove the N-terminal His6–SUMO tag. The gene encoding the designed VchTnsA variant D1A was cloned into the pARZ4 expression vector encoding an N-terminal His6 tag and carrying a chloramphenicol resistance marker. The plasmid was transformed into BL21 cells, and protein expression was carried out under the same growth and induction conditions described for VchTnsB. Sources indicate that for MBP-affinity purification, approximately 2 ml amylose resin was equilibrated with 5 column volumes of MBP lysis buffer and loaded into a gravity flow column. Prior to heparin chromatography, pooled amylose fractions were diluted with heparin dilution buffer to reduce the NaCl concentration below 200 mM. The diluted sample was loaded onto a 1 ml heparin column equilibrated in heparin binding buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 200 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol), washed with 15–20 column volumes of binding buffer, and eluted with a linear salt gradient to heparin elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 1.1 M NaCl, 5% glycerol). During size-exclusion chromatography, a substantial fraction of the protein eluted in the column void volume, consistent with aggregation, whereas only a small proportion eluted as the expected monodisperse species. Consequently, recovery of purified TnsAB following size-exclusion chromatography was limited. Protein concentration was determined by Bradford assay. Final samples were aliquoted, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C.

It has been revealed that recombinant IHF heterodimer was produced using the pACYCDuet-1-ihfαβ expression plasmid (a gift from the Nuñez laboratory), in which the ihfa and ihfb genes, amplified from E. coli BL21 genomic DNA (gDNA), were cloned into the pACYCDuet-1 backbone (Novagen). The VchCascade–TniQ complex was produced using a pHelper-based plasmid encoding Cas8/5, Cas7, Cas6, His6-tagged TniQ, and a CRISPR RNA (crRNA)–ffsx6 array encoding a ccdB-targeting guide RNA. The Cascade–TniQ complex was initially captured via the His6 tag on TniQ using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography following the same purification protocol as performed for designed VchTnsA. Pooled elution fractions were subjected to anion-exchange chromatography on a Mono Q column (Cytiva) pre-equilibrated in binding buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT). Proteins were eluted over a linear NaCl gradient to 1 M in elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 1,000 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT), and fractions containing the Cascade–TniQ complex were identified by SDS–PAGE, pooled and concentrated.

Expression and purification were carried out identically to the procedure described above, with tag-free Cascade–TniQ obtained following overnight Ulp1 digestion after Ni-NTA and Mono Q chromatography.
